opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the places where the choice of rank-one components really bites, so it's worth being careful about.

A rank-one matrix is just an outer product, u v-transpose. Mechanistically, it reads off one direction in the input, the v direction, takes the dot product, and writes that scalar out along one direction u in the output. That's all it can do. It's a read-one-direction, write-one-direction operation.

A genuine rotation, even the simplest one in a 2D plane, isn't like that. It takes x to some mix of x and y, and y to some mix of y and minus x, at the same time. That needs at least rank two. You cannot express it with a single outer product, no matter how you choose u and v.

So in stochastic parameter decomposition, if the network is doing something rotation-like, what we expect is that the decomposition finds multiple rank-one subcomponents that always switch on together. The causal importance function learns that whenever one is needed, the others are too, because ablating any one of them alone breaks the computation. In that case you'd want to group them and say, together these form one mechanism, a rotation in this subspace.

That's a known limitation. We picked rank one because it's the most atomic unit you can have, which gives you good minimality and makes subcomponents easy to interpret individually. But it means some computations that are naturally higher-rank, rotations being the cleanest example, get split into pieces that only make sense jointly. One response is clustering co-activating subcomponents afterwards. Another is allowing higher-rank components from the start, which trades away some of that atomicity.

And I think that's actually informative. When you see a tight cluster of rank-one components that always fire together, it's a signal that the network is doing something inherently multidimensional there, like a rotation, rather than a bunch of independent feature reads and writes. So the limitation becomes a diagnostic, as long as you know to look for it.

r001.rationale: It explains that a rank-one matrix reads the input’s component along direction v and writes that scalar along direction u.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that comes up a lot when we're thinking about decomposing networks into parameter components, and I think the honest answer starts with: a single rank-one matrix can't really represent a rotation at all. A rank-one matrix is an outer product, u v-transpose. What it does is read off one direction in the input space, measure how much of the input lies along v, and then write that scalar out along a single direction u in the output space. So it has a one-dimensional image. A rotation, by contrast, is full rank, it preserves norms, it maps a whole subspace onto itself. There's just no way to get that out of one rank-one piece.

What you can get is a rotation as a sum of rank-one pieces. If you've got, say, a 2D rotation acting on some plane, you can write that as two rank-one terms, or you can decompose it as a sum of outer products in various other ways. And I think this is actually where it gets interesting from a decomposition standpoint, because the question becomes: what's the "right" set of rank-one components to describe that rotation? And there isn't a unique answer. The SVD gives you one, with orthogonal singular vectors, but you could equally well pick a non-orthogonal basis for the plane and get a different set of rank-one terms that sum to the same matrix.

Where this matters for interpretability is things like positional representations, or anything that looks like a Fourier-style structure, where the network is genuinely doing something rotation-like. In modular addition, for instance, the network is rotating around a circle. If your decomposition method is biased toward finding rank-one components, it'll shatter that rotation into pieces, and each individual piece isn't really a meaningful unit of computation on its own. The meaningful unit is the whole rank-two block.

So the way I've come to think about it is that rank-one components are the right atoms when the mechanism really is "read one direction, write one direction," which is a lot of what happens in networks. But you need your method to be able to group those atoms into higher-rank components when the network is actually using a subspace as a unit. In our work on attribution-based decomposition, that's partly why we care about identifying components by how they're used in the forward pass, rather than purely by their linear algebraic structure. If two rank-one pieces are always active together, always attributed together, that's a signal they're really one component, a rotation or whatever it is, not two. The linear algebra on its own just can't tell you that.

r001.rationale: It says a rank-one matrix measures the input’s component along v and writes that scalar along u.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish rotating a particular direction from rotating the whole space. A rank-one matrix can be written as an outer product, u v transpose. Applied to an input, it takes the component along v and produces an output along u, with some scaling. So those input and output directions can have any angle between them.

In that sense, it can represent a change in direction. But it’s not a rotation in the usual geometric sense, because it collapses everything orthogonal to v. It doesn’t preserve the geometry of the whole space.

When you decompose a neural network’s weight matrix into rank-one terms, each term describes one of these input-to-output mappings. The sum can implement a full rotation, or something much more general, even though each individual term only has a one-dimensional output.

r001.rationale: It says the matrix takes the input component along v and produces an output along u, with scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish a rank-one matrix from a rotation in the usual geometric sense. A rank-one matrix can be written as an outer product, say u v transpose. Applied to an input, it takes the component along v and produces an output along u, scaled by how much of that component was present. So you can think of it as reading in one direction and writing in another.

If those directions differ, there’s a sense in which it redirects information. But it isn’t a general rotation: it collapses all the other input directions. A genuine rotation preserves the geometry of the whole space, and generally requires multiple rank-one terms to represent.

For neural network decomposition, the interesting question is whether those individual read-and-write operations correspond to meaningful pieces of computation. You can always decompose a matrix mathematically; finding a decomposition that tells you what the network is actually doing is the harder part.

r001.rationale: It says a rank-one matrix reads the input component along v and produces an output along u, scaled by that component.
